question: data center water usage
answer_text:
Water use by data centers turns heavily on the cooling technology chosen. In Cheyenne, officials traced local experience back to a 2009 greenhouse data center and a larger Microsoft facility in the North Range Business Park about 14 years ago, reporting that existing data centers use 200 acre feet of water annually and that all data centers combined account for 1.48% of water sold by the board of public utilities [1]. The same testimony described a shift away from water-intensive evaporative cooling of server rooms toward cooling the chips themselves, with closed-loop systems at two facilities under construction requiring roughly two acre feet to charge the system and then recirculating that water for up to six years, and new air-cooled systems using no water at all [1]. A Bartow County witness gave comparable framing, saying open-loop systems use millions of gallons while closed-loop uses about 10% of that, with a typical closed-loop average data center at about 300,000 gallons a day, equivalent to roughly a thousand homes [3]. In Louisa County, Edgecor's Shannon Hill facility was described as a closed-loop air-cooled system using very little water, equivalent to only 35 homes at full buildout, and not connected to the Northeast Creek Reservoir, with any drought restrictions applying to data centers the same as to other LCWA customers [5].

Monitoring and accountability were recurring themes. Cheyenne utility staff said every connection into a data center is metered, including fire loops, and that smart meters and gateways installed 10 to 12 years ago allow real-time readings as often as hourly, with alarms for high usage [8]. Opponents elsewhere pressed for firmer limits: a Culpeper speaker asked how the county would monitor water use and what would happen in a drought for a project relying on wells, urging the applicant to commit to a maximum daily and annual withdrawal [2]. The Piedmont Environmental Council argued that of five unbuilt approved campuses in the water and sewer service area, only one had proffered any limited water usage, putting the municipal supply at risk if facilities chose evaporative cooling, still the cheapest option [4]. Another Culpeper speaker cited Loudoun County, where potable water use for cooling was said to be up 250% from the prior year and over 100 million gallons are supplied to keep approved data centers cool [6]. In Cass County, Iowa, residents organizing as a data center watch coalition listed water usage among their concerns as commissioners voted for a pause on new data centers [7].

answer_text:
Across these records, rezoning applications appear at various stages of approval. In Newton County, Georgia, a parcel near Flat Rock Road and Gregory Road, part of parcel 0079009 and adjacent to property already in the city of Covington, came before the board in June for a rezoning to the M2 industrial district, and the board approved that rezoning subject to a number of conditions, with the applicant JBW Investments later applying to annex the property and intending to zone it to Covington's M2 classification [8]. In Caroline County, Virginia, a board approved a rezoning for MC Deed off Dry Bridge Road on the west side of an existing development, with a second rezoning at the intersection of Coleman's Mill and Route 207 following, the Dry Bridge Road rezoning having been expedited after the applicant's design priorities shifted [2]. Also in Caroline County, two of three parcels in application Z-01-2008 were previously approved by the board, with parcel 82-8-121 held out pending a public hearing, and the previously accepted proffers remaining unchanged [4].

Officials in these meetings drew limits around what approval means. A Bartow County, Georgia, speaker emphasized that submissions by a rezoning applicant serve only the rezoning and its stipulations, so anything pictured that does not comply with development regulations, county ordinances, or state or federal law—such as hammerhead cul-de-sacs—is not approved or implicitly approved even if the planning commission recommends approval [1]. In Caroline County, it was clarified that a rezoning and accompanying special exceptions are distinct matters, so the rezoning could be approved without the two special exception permits, though if the rezoning is not approved the special exceptions cannot proceed [6]. In Madison County, Mississippi, a member questioned the sequence of actions, asking whether Planning and Zoning approved the rezoning of certain property before or after approving the comprehensive plan [5].

Opposition also features in the record. question: substation transmission upgrade
answer_text:
Across several jurisdictions, public bodies have discussed substation and transmission upgrade projects at differing voltages and stages. In Culpeper County, Virginia, a utility described an existing north–south corridor carrying 115 kilovolt and 230 kilovolt lines, and identified a project need for one new double circuit 230 kilovolt transmission line and four new substations in the Culpeper Tech Zone, along with upgrades to 115 kilovolt lines in Fauquier County and part of Culpeper [1]. A related rationale was laid out in Orange County, Virginia, where the existing 115,000 volt line from the Remington substation to Gordonsville was said to be old and, based on PJM information, headed for overload conditions by 2018, so a higher voltage with greater capacity was proposed; officials noted that simply building a 230,000 volt line without moving customers off the 115 kilovolt system would not by itself increase reliability [8].

In Nevada, a presentation to a Reno-area body described a 525 kV proposed Green Lake West line running between the Las Vegas area and the Walker River substation being constructed just north of Yerington in Lyon County, plus "Common Tie" facilities consisting of three 345 kV lines emanating west and northwest from that substation, one terminating at NV Energy's existing Mira Loma substation in Reno, and a third component, Green Lake North, another 525 kV line [3]. In San Antonio, the CPS Energy board adopted the PUC's selection in docket 51023 of route Z2 to substation site 7 on Toutant Beauregard Road, roughly a half mile west of Scenic Loop Road, after a process involving geographically diverse routes, landowner notification, and testimony on need and environmental impact [5]. The board approved construction of the Scenic Loop substation and transmission project with associated transmission and distribution lines, substation communication systems, and easement, fee simple, and property exchange acquisitions, by negotiation or eminent domain [6][7], and directed staff to keep the project site map publicly available before a motion to proceed with land acquisition and construction [7].

Elsewhere, Stillwater, Oklahoma trustees took up approval of the GRDA Stillwater 69 substation to Jardot transmission replacement project, with staff explaining that the city's electric utility operates a 69,000 volt transmission loop, built of poles and related infrastructure, that supplies five electrical substations [4]. In Mesa, Arizona, an official described taking transmission from WAPA under Network Integrated Transmission Service with delivery points at named substations including West Wing and Pinnacle Peak, noted transmission costs had fallen from about $2.5 million a year to roughly $1 million, and acknowledged the lingering risk that if Western upgrades its system Mesa could be billed for it, a charge the city would contest unless reasonable and caused by Mesa [2].

answer_text:
Across several jurisdictions, public bodies have discussed substation and transmission upgrade projects at differing voltages and stages. In Culpeper County, Virginia, a utility described an existing north–south corridor carrying 115 kilovolt and 230 kilovolt lines, and identified a project need for one new double circuit 230 kilovolt transmission line and four new substations in the Culpeper Tech Zone, along with upgrades to 115 kilovolt lines in Fauquier County and part of Culpeper [1]. A related rationale was laid out in Orange County, Virginia, where the existing 115,000 volt line from the Remington substation to Gordonsville was said to be old and, based on PJM information, headed for overload conditions by 2018, so a higher voltage with greater capacity was proposed; officials noted that simply building a 230,000 volt line without moving customers off the 115 kilovolt system would not by itself increase reliability [8].

In Nevada, a presentation to a Reno-area body described a 525 kV proposed Green Lake West line running between the Las Vegas area and the Walker River substation being constructed just north of Yerington in Lyon County, plus "Common Tie" facilities consisting of three 345 kV lines emanating west and northwest from that substation, one terminating at NV Energy's existing Mira Loma substation in Reno, and a third component, Green Lake North, another 525 kV line [3]. In San Antonio, the CPS Energy board adopted the PUC's selection in docket 51023 of route Z2 to substation site 7 on Toutant Beauregard Road, roughly a half mile west of Scenic Loop Road, after a process involving geographically diverse routes, landowner notification, and testimony on need and environmental impact [5]. The board approved construction of the Scenic Loop substation and transmission project with associated transmission and distribution lines, substation communication systems, and easement, fee simple, and property exchange acquisitions, by negotiation or eminent domain [6][7], and directed staff to keep the project site map publicly available before a motion to proceed with land acquisition and construction [7].

Elsewhere, Stillwater, Oklahoma trustees took up approval of the GRDA Stillwater 69 substation to Jardot transmission replacement project, with staff explaining that the city's electric utility operates a 69,000 volt transmission loop, built of poles and related infrastructure, that supplies five electrical substations [4]. In Mesa, Arizona, an official described taking transmission from WAPA under Network Integrated Transmission Service with delivery points at named substations including West Wing and Pinnacle Peak, noted transmission costs had fallen from about $2.5 million a year to roughly $1 million, and acknowledged the lingering risk that if Western upgrades its system Mesa could be billed for it, a charge the city would contest unless reasonable and caused by Mesa [2].

question: tax abatement incentives data center
answer_text:
In Temple, Texas, the city council may consider designating a tax abatement zone and authorizing an abatement when at least two criteria under its adopted economic development policy are met [2], a framework tied to the two factors allowed under Texas tax code chapter 312 [3]. An early example was an application from Temple Green Data seeking abatement of a percentage of the increases in taxable value on an approximately 33-acre site in Synergy Park just west of Bob White Road, with the company planning to invest at least $225 million in improvements for a data center and to create at least 20 new full-time jobs [2]. More recently, staff received an application from Rowan Temple LLC proposing a hyperscale data center with an investment of $700 million in construction and 40 new jobs, with the proposed incentive being a 10-year ad valorem abatement of 50% on the increase in real and personal property [3]. Officials explained that the $700 million commitment is the total for the project, inclusive of real property improvements by the developer, who may also use personal property improvements done directly or through an affiliate or tenant, but the developer remains responsible for the total capital investment and all requirements of the agreement [1]. If the minimum capital investment or job creation numbers are not met, or continuous operation as a data center is not maintained through the full term, the abatement is void and the benefit is not received [1]. The term of the contract is 10 years, and the developer can do more but not less [1]. Temple officials have also noted that the city does not control ERCOT, Oncor, state electric policy, state tax incentives, or the broader legal framework around private property rights in Texas, while it does hold local tools such as annexation, zoning, noise mitigation, traffic review, infrastructure requirements, utility agreements, and other enforceable contracts, and council members have asked how often abatements are granted generally, not just for data centers [8].

Elsewhere, in Ohio it was stated that JobsOhio and its network of economic development organizations do not provide incentives to data centers, though local tax abatements are a local government-by-local government consideration determining whether a data center pays property tax, alongside employment taxes and a kilowatt-hour tax on electricity that partly flows to local schools [4]. In Reno, a speaker noted that the tax abatement also applies to sales taxes, reducing the sales tax to 2% if the developer complies with conditions such as employing a certain number of workers at certain pay levels, requirements described as lenient enough that most data centers would meet them, making substantial tax generation for the city unlikely [5]. In Douglas County, Georgia, an official said incentives should be negotiated on the front end because a data center already operating cannot be required to renegotiate its existing abatement, citing an AWS partnership whose incentive required community give-backs such as think big spaces for schools, STEM centers, a park, and tree planting, and indicating future abatement and incentive agreements would include more of that [7].

question: data center noise complaints
answer_text:
Data center noise has surfaced repeatedly in public comment as a distinct kind of nuisance, one that residents describe as low-pitched and constant rather than intermittently loud. In Culpeper County, a speaker cited a study attributed to Dr. John Liver, described as a former NSA scientist, stating that data center noise typically travels two and a half miles, and argued that clustering approved data centers together produces a cumulative effect comparable to a mass campus like the one in Manassas — likened to the difference between one lawnmower and four running at once, or one party in a neighborhood versus four [1]. Another resident, Charlotte Cole, urged council members who had not accepted an offer to visit a Manassas data center to instead visit the Great Oak neighborhood in Prince William County, where data centers have generated consistent complaints about low-pitched roars and tinny screeches, which she considered a more comparable scenario [2]. She also pointed to the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission's year-long study on data centers, released the prior day [2].

That report's chapter six, as read into the record, explains that most local noise limits are defined using A-weighted decibels, a metric targeting excessively loud sources such as parties and barking dogs, so the lower-frequency noise data centers emit is not fully captured; as a result, data center noise rarely exceeds ordinance limits even though its constancy is problematic for residents, and localities could adopt a supplemental limit using a metric such as C-weighted decibels [3]. Earlier Culpeper testimony had recorded significant public concern during a rezoning period that noise from a data center, specifically its cooling facilities, would exceed that of a residential community [6]. In a later Culpeper meeting, a speaker presented a model developed by the late Dr. John Liver, described there as a NASA scientist who devoted much of his retirement to data center noise and who based the model on data centers in Prince William County; the concern raised for Copper Ridge was cumulative noise from both campuses even if each operated within allowable limits, potentially raising the baseline on East Davis Street from roughly 50 dBA to over 60 dBA, a doubling of ambient noise that could affect how downtown Culpeper sounds and feels and reduce its appeal as a travel destination [8].

Similar dynamics appear elsewhere. In St. Joseph County, Indiana, staff described noise regulation as a frequent and sometimes intense nationwide issue where industrial development is approved near residential areas, particularly alongside data center expansion, with written complaints ranging from dozens at smaller or remote sites to hundreds or thousands in highly visible locations, and residents in Indiana collecting thousands of petition signatures against development and for moratoriums [4][7]. The speaker anticipated more pushback and a crescendo of formal complaints given the scale of industrial development, noted that the existing ordinance language left unclear who in local government administers it, and framed the goal as broader community acceptance built on trust [4]. That effort began with a filing in December following a November distribution to county staff that drew little feedback, and has since involved extensive stakeholder and staff engagement [7]. In DeKalb County, Illinois, a member speaking from prior experience receiving code enforcement complaints favored a single standard and methodology based on decibel meter readings, supported hiring more code enforcement or police officers and training them, and noted data showing roughly one or two complaints per day over the past two years while asking for a map of where those complaints originate [5].

Another resident, Charlotte Cole, urged council members who had not accepted an offer to visit a Manassas data center to instead visit the Great Oak neighborhood in Prince William County, where data centers have generated consistent complaints about low-pitched roars and tinny screeches, which she considered a more comparable scenario [2]. She also pointed to the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission's year-long study on data centers, released the prior day [2].

question: data center moratorium
answer_text: Calls for data center moratoriums have surfaced in multiple jurisdictions. In San Antonio, several city council members, including District 6 Councilman Rick Galvan, gathered on the City Hall steps to call for a pause on all new data center construction, arguing that zoning and land use codes should benefit working class residents rather than tech billionaires, and citing concerns over water use, land use, noise, and pollution as two new data centers are built on the far west side [1]. That same block notes Governor Abbott ordered audits that stop new ERCOT-contained data center approvals until agencies verify certain community impact details [1]. In St. Joseph County, Indiana, a petition asked the County Council to assess the impact of current hyperscale data centers and to enact protective policy, and, until that work was complete, to impose a moratorium on improvement location permits under negotiation, new permits, or expansions across all zoning districts in the unincorporated areas [2]. A speaker there urged a moratorium of at least a year on all data center development countywide, noting a six-month pause was set to expire on June 9 and that further moratoriums could follow [3]. At a later meeting, a commenter pointed to the Marshall County Commissioners, who moved from a moratorium to a total ban, and asked St. Joseph County commissioners to go on record recommending a complete ban [7]. In Reno, a speaker supported a moratorium on consideration of data center projects until data center code requirements are thoroughly fleshed out and finalized, disputing staff's comparison of data centers to warehouses and criticizing an administrative decision that did not address resource usage, energy requirements, environmental impacts, limited employment, or sustainability [4]. In Newton County, Georgia, officials asked legal counsel whether the term "data centers" in the resolution would cover server farms and any technicality, and were told the commonly understood term as reasonably interpreted under zoning law would apply, though a commissioner warned that annexation by Social Circle could render county moratoriums moot in the southeastern part of the county [5]. Newton County officials also discussed House Bill 1059, a state data center moratorium running from July 1, 2026 to December 31, 2028, which would also establish a data center impact assessment commission to study impacts and recommend a statewide zoning ordinance or model local ordinance [8]. In Oklahoma, a resident filed a petition for a moratorium that could extend up to two years and sought 2,500 signatures, though a floodplain administrator who also serves as emergency manager said the moratorium would not have teeth in the city and that the county's only land development jurisdiction is through the floodplain, requiring hydrology and hydrostatic studies showing no adverse effects [6].

answer_text: Calls for data center moratoriums have surfaced in multiple jurisdictions. In San Antonio, several city council members, including District 6 Councilman Rick Galvan, gathered on the City Hall steps to call for a pause on all new data center construction, arguing that zoning and land use codes should benefit working class residents rather than tech billionaires, and citing concerns over water use, land use, noise, and pollution as two new data centers are built on the far west side [1]. That same block notes Governor Abbott ordered audits that stop new ERCOT-contained data center approvals until agencies verify certain community impact details [1]. In St. Joseph County, Indiana, a petition asked the County Council to assess the impact of current hyperscale data centers and to enact protective policy, and, until that work was complete, to impose a moratorium on improvement location permits under negotiation, new permits, or expansions across all zoning districts in the unincorporated areas [2]. A speaker there urged a moratorium of at least a year on all data center development countywide, noting a six-month pause was set to expire on June 9 and that further moratoriums could follow [3]. At a later meeting, a commenter pointed to the Marshall County Commissioners, who moved from a moratorium to a total ban, and asked St. Joseph County commissioners to go on record recommending a complete ban [7]. In Reno, a speaker supported a moratorium on consideration of data center projects until data center code requirements are thoroughly fleshed out and finalized, disputing staff's comparison of data centers to warehouses and criticizing an administrative decision that did not address resource usage, energy requirements, environmental impacts, limited employment, or sustainability [4]. In Newton County, Georgia, officials asked legal counsel whether the term "data centers" in the resolution would cover server farms and any technicality, and were told the commonly understood term as reasonably interpreted under zoning law would apply, though a commissioner warned that annexation by Social Circle could render county moratoriums moot in the southeastern part of the county [5]. Newton County officials also discussed House Bill 1059, a state data center moratorium running from July 1, 2026 to December 31, 2028, which would also establish a data center impact assessment commission to study impacts and recommend a statewide zoning ordinance or model local ordinance [8]. In Oklahoma, a resident filed a petition for a moratorium that could extend up to two years and sought 2,500 signatures, though a floodplain administrator who also serves as emergency manager said the moratorium would not have teeth in the city and that the county's only land development jurisdiction is through the floodplain, requiring hydrology and hydrostatic studies showing no adverse effects [6].

question: grid capacity interconnection queue
answer_text:
Across these records, the interconnection queue appears as a gating step for new generation and load. A Cheyenne, Wyoming discussion described a federal "queue" in which a developer must present a project and get in line, working up toward getting onto the grid to produce power, with the queue processed in order to see who is ready to produce [4]. In ERCOT, testimony noted over 1,700 active generation interconnection requests totaling almost 350 gigawatts, a figure described as very dynamic and changing daily, and the speaker cautioned that historically the ERCOT queue is very fluid and not all requests come to fruition [3]. That same San Antonio presentation framed Texas as the second leading market outside Virginia for data centers and large loads, driven in part by a friendly business climate [3]. Earlier San Antonio testimony described a portfolio of aging generation with mostly intermittent wind and solar being added, a very light level of battery capacity limited by short duration, and a legislative session that did not address market design for adding capacity or whether additional interconnection to other grids was needed for flexibility during problems on the ERCOT system [2].

On the demand side, a later San Antonio discussion tied data center availability promises — some seeking "five nines," roughly 79 seconds of downtime per quarter — to major implications for power supply, transmission, grid interconnection, and cooling, and observed that developers want a very fast interconnection and permitting process [5]. In St. Joseph County, Indiana, a speaker explained that the county sits between the MISO grid, which covers most of Indiana and is associated with NIPSCO, and the PJM grid associated with Indiana Michigan and AES, so power can easily be sent to one grid or the other, creating a capacity opportunity given infrastructure placed in western St. Joseph County [1]. In Pittsylvania County, Virginia, a solar applicant described analyzing the electric grid and moving through the PJM interconnection process into its final stages, alongside extensive environmental studies, and looking for sites that can interconnect to move power to commercial and residential customers while limiting negative local impacts [6]. The same county heard that major connections are inside cabinets and all wire is buried except for the interconnection to the grid [7][8].

Reuse water — wastewater treatment discharge that would typically flow to a stream — was presented in Caroline County, Virginia as a way to supply industrial cooling for data centers [2]. Cooling for data centers is described as a seasonal issue, with typical usage over a six- to seven-month period from April through October and little to no usage from November through March, and the figures data centers provide represent a maximum or peak day that occurs roughly 7 to 10 days out of a year [2]. Caroline County has a 1.5 million gallon a day wastewater treatment plant permitted to go to 3 million gallons a day [2], and going beyond 3 MGD requires nitrogen and phosphorus allocations, for which DEQ's requirements were summarized as reuse, reuse, and reuse [3]. The plant is characterized as performing beyond state-of-the-art, though its current low average discharge of 413,000 gallons a day is not keeping up [3]. Because roughly 75% of cooling water evaporates and 25% returns to the wastewater treatment plant, 100,000 gallons a day supplied yields 25,000 gallons returned that can be reused again [3]. Adding 25% of the current return gives 103,000 gallons, with a total cooling water figure of 56,000 gallons the county could supply today, and projected growth of 20,000 gallons for commercial and 20,000 gallons for homes over twelve years approaches almost a half million gallons of new use, producing nearly 600,000 gallons a day of cooling water [4]. Data center buildings were estimated at about 100 employees per building across three shifts, with EPA's estimate of 20 gallons per day per employee [4].

Elsewhere, reclamation facilities describe similar reuse aims: the Jomax Water Reclamation facility in Peoria treats sewage from residential and commercial users and repurposes it as reclamation water for golf courses, parks, schools, and roadways, expanding from 2.25 million gallons a day toward 3, then 4, then 6 million gallons a day, with plans to connect all three wastewater plants by a common reuse pipeline [1]. Chandler's Ocotillo facility likewise cleans wastewater in aeration tanks using bacteria so it can be reused in the city [8]. Reno's project would take water already treated at the Reno water reclamation facility — currently going to reuse or recycled water landscaping projects and Swan Lake — treat it to potable standards, and inject it underground for extraction after six months [7]. Columbus's Division of Water Reclamation treats more than 590 million gallons per day during wet weather and beneficially reuses 100% of its biosolids [5]. Intel's on-site water treatment and reclamation facility treats water for reuse in the factory or support systems or for discharge back to the municipality for reuse there, part of a goal to be net positive for water by 2030 [6].

question: electric rate increase data center load growth
answer_text:
Across several jurisdictions, officials have tied electric load growth to data centers and, in some cases, to rate impacts. In Nevada, a large projected statewide load growth led the PUCN to approve two new gas peaking power plants at the Valmy coal-fired station, projected to cost ratepayers about $573 million, described as a substantial ratepayer investment going toward energy associated with data centers, particularly in Northern Nevada [6]. That testimony framed the result as a large cost shift onto ratepayers from infrastructure tied to AI and data centers, a pattern said to be occurring across the Western United States with rates rising to pay for the investments needed to power data centers [6].
